verdicts.outcome_rationale: This is a genuine agent-fault failure—the verifier's FAIL is correct. The GSO harness graded the patch against 20 hidden merge benchmarks and reported opt_commit=False with continuous reward 0.28, below the pass threshold of 1.20 on gm_speedup_patch_commit [1][2]. The instruction asked to optimize pd.merge_ordered on sorted monotonic keys while preserving functional equivalence and pursuing the best possible speedup [3]. The agent profiled the merge path, edited pandas/core/algorithms.py (O(n) inverse permutation in safe_sort) and pandas/core/reshape/merge.py (assume_unique in _sort_labels; skip redundant _factorize_keys for single-key joins), synced the files into the venv, and self-tested ~3.1x speedup (~0.286s to ~0.090s) with byte-identical outputs across 31 hand-written scenarios before stopping [4][5]. The held-out verifier applied that patch cleanly, all 20 equivalence checks passed, and timings on the instruction-matching workload (gso_test_3: large sorted-key merge_ordered inner join) dropped from ~0.28s baseline to ~0.09s patched—roughly matching the agent's claim—but the reference commit 061c2e9190 ("PERF: merge on monotonic keys") still ran the same test at ~0.006s, leaving the patch ~15x slower than the known solution and yielding gm_speedup_patch_commit≈0.28 [6][7]. The agent never found the monotonic-key fast path that dominates this scenario; its micro-optimizations to factorization/sorting are real and correct but insufficient for a task gated on near-reference performance, so TN stands.

verdicts.outcome_rationale: This is a genuine agent-fault failure where the verifier's FAIL is correct. The GSO verifier reported binary_reward 0 with a continuous gm_speedup_patch_commit score of 0.643, below the 1.20 pass threshold and with opt_commit false [1][2][3][4]. The task asked the agent to optimize pandas merge_ordered performance while preserving functional equivalence and pursuing the best possible speedup [5]. The agent added a `_maybe_get_sorted_unique_inner_result` fast path in `pandas/core/reshape/merge.py` that uses `np.searchsorted` for inner merges on a single sorted unique key [6], reinstalled pandas, and declared success after seeing roughly 40× improvement on the provided benchmark versus the unpatched base (~0.27s to ~0.006s) plus 20 passing merge_ordered unit tests [7]. The hidden verifier confirmed correctness—all 20 benchmark scripts passed equivalence checks after the patch [8]—but measured the patch against a known upstream optimization at commit 061c2e9 and found the agent slower on the headline case (test 0 mean ~0.007s patch vs ~0.004s commit) and ~0.64× on the geometric-mean commit/patch metric overall [9][4]. The agent never had access to that reference commit or the held-out 20-test suite, and its self-checks were limited to the single instruction benchmark and installed unit tests, so it concluded success without meeting the task's performance bar [7][8]. Because correctness was preserved but required speed relative to the reference solution was not achieved, this is TN, not FN.

judge_verdict.summary: The agent delivered a partial monotonic join fast-path that aces the prompt benchmark but falls well short of the reference commit on held-out workloads, so the verifier's FAIL is correct.

verdicts.outcome_rationale: This is a genuine agent-fault failure—the verifier's FAIL is correct. The GSO harness compared the agent patch against baseline and reference commit 061c2e9190 ("PERF: merge on monotonic keys"), reporting opt_commit=False, continuous reward 0.867, and binary_reward 0 because reward did not exceed the 1.20 pass threshold [1][2][3]. The task asked for general merge_ordered speedups while preserving correctness and pursuing the best possible speedup [4], but the agent's final change is only a narrow monotonic fast-path in get_join_indexers that calls libjoin.*_join_indexer after ndarray monotonicity checks and only when at least one key side is unique [5]. That direction suffices for the instruction benchmark—the agent measured 0.2577s before patching [6] and celebrated ~0.0039s afterward [7]—and the hidden verifier confirms test 0 dropping from ~0.29s to ~0.004s, matching the reference commit on that workload [8]. However, on broader held-out scenarios the patch stalls far short of the reference: test 14 (multi-merge workload with NaN-laced, duplicate float keys) stays ~0.75s versus ~0.77s baseline while the reference commit runs ~0.46s, and test 15 shows the same pattern (~0.65s patch vs ~0.43s commit) [9][10], yielding the sub-threshold gm_speedup_patch_commit score. The agent never saw these tests and relied on its own benchmark plus pandas merge unit tests, which was insufficient to catch the large generalization gap [6][7]. The reference commit is a broader merge refactor beyond the agent's single fast-path block, and the verifier benchmarks against that full commit [3]. Outcome is TN: verifier correctly failed a partial optimization that does not truly meet the task's performance bar.
